passage:
Tuesday. "Homework done, Papa!" Rajni called, already reaching for the remote. The maths sheet was done. The English essay was two lines long, tucked under her pillow. Her father, Kamal, smiled and let her watch cartoons.
Thursday. A note came home in her school diary: Essay not submitted. Papa held it out. "You said homework was done." "I did do homework," Rajni said, and her voice went small. "I did the maths." "Did you tell me the whole thing?" he asked. She looked at the floor. She hadn't said one false word, but she knew what he had believed.
Saturday. "Papa, maths is done, but my essay is only half. Can you sit with me?" He pulled up a chair.

qa.q: Where was Rajni's English essay on Tuesday?
qa.a: The essay was two lines long, tucked under her pillow.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when Papa asked, "Did you tell me the whole thing?"
qa.a: She felt ashamed; her voice went small and she looked at the floor, knowing he had believed something untrue even though she hadn't said a false word.

qa.q: What changed in what Rajni said on Saturday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She gave the whole picture, maths done and essay only half, and asked for help, so her father could respond to the full truth.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt when the teacher's note came home?
qa.a: He may have felt misled and a bit let down, since he let her watch cartoons believing all her homework was finished.

grounding: A girl tells her father her homework is done while leaving out the unfinished essay, and slowly learns that misleading by silence counts.

passage:
Zainab beta, your Gurpreet Aunty has a story for you. You said you had packed your bag for the trip, and there's no water bottle in it. That reminds me. When I was nine, in our village, my job was to feed the two goats before school. One cold morning I gave them water, skipped the fodder, and told my mother, "Done, Bebe, I fed them." Water is food of a kind, I told myself.
By afternoon the goats were bleating so loudly that a neighbour came over. Bebe didn't shout. She just asked, "Gurpreet, which part did you leave out?" My face went hot. I hadn't said anything false, but I had let her believe something false. The goats went hungry all day because of my clever little sentence.

qa.q: What was young Gurpreet's job before school?
qa.a: Gurpreet's job was to feed the two goats before school.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when Bebe asked which part was left out?
qa.a: She felt ashamed; her face went hot because she knew she had let Bebe believe something false.

qa.q: Which choice did Bebe make when the goats were bleating, and why did it help?
qa.a: Bebe didn't shout but asked which part Gurpreet left out, which let Gurpreet see for herself that misleading by silence counts.

qa.q: How might Bebe have felt when she heard the goats bleating all afternoon?
qa.a: She probably felt worried for the hungry goats and misled by Gurpreet's "Done", yet she chose a calm question over shouting.

grounding: An aunty recalls a childhood morning when she left out the key part of a chore, showing a child learning that a true-enough sentence can still mislead.

passage:
At six, Harish sat at the long table with his maths sheet finished and his English workbook still closed under it. When his mother Kavitha came in with her office bag, she asked the question she asked every day.
"Homework done?"
"I finished the maths sheet," Harish said, holding it up. That part was true.
"Good boy." She smiled, tired, and zipped his bag without looking inside.
On the auto ride home, Harish watched the traffic and felt the closed workbook pressing through the bag against his back. He hadn't said a single false word. So why did his stomach feel tight?
"Amma," he said at the signal, "the English isn't done. I only said the maths part."
She looked at him for a moment, then nodded. "Thank you for telling me the whole thing."

qa.q: What was still closed under Harish's maths sheet?
qa.a: His English workbook was still closed under it.

qa.q: Why did Harish's stomach feel tight on the auto ride?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and guilty, because although every word was true, he knew his mother believed all the homework was done.

qa.q: What small step did Harish take that helped?
qa.a: He told his mother at the signal that the English wasn't done, giving her the whole picture instead of the part that sounded good.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel when Harish tells her the whole thing?
qa.a: She might feel surprised but grateful and proud, because he chose to fill in what his silence had left out.

grounding: It shows a child saying a true part about homework while hiding the unfinished part, and learning that misleading by silence counts.

passage:
Monday evening. Mumma called from the kitchen, "Anjali, is your science model done?" Anjali looked at the half-painted volcano on the floor. The base was ready; the top was still bare cardboard. "I did the model," she said. Mumma said, "Wonderful," and went back to the rotis.
Wednesday. Her little sister Gargi poked the volcano. "It's not finished. You told Mumma you did it." Anjali snapped, "I said I did the model. I didn't say I finished it." Gargi frowned. "That's a trick answer."
Friday morning. The model was due. Anjali stood at the kitchen door holding the half-painted volcano. "Mumma, on Monday I said I did it. I only did half. I let you think I finished."
Mumma put down the ladle. "So let's see what we can do in the next twenty minutes." Together they painted the top grey.

qa.q: What was still bare cardboard on the volcano?
qa.a: The top was still bare cardboard.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she snapped at Gargi?
qa.a: She felt defensive and a little guilty, because Gargi had named the "trick answer" she was already uneasy about.

qa.q: What worked on Friday morning?
qa.a: Anjali told Mumma plainly that she had only done half and had let her think it was finished, and Mumma helped her finish quickly.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Anjali's answer to Mumma?
qa.a: Gargi sees it as a trick answer, because the words were true but they made Mumma believe something false.

grounding: It shows a child saying the model was done when only half was, and slowly seeing that misleading by leaving things out still counts.

passage:
Asif, you keep saying "but I did do my homework." Listen to a story from your Vasudha Aunty first. When I was about your age, in our old house near the railway colony, my father used to ask every night, "Sums done?" and I would say, "Yes, Baba, I did my sums." I had done the first five. There were ten.
I thought I was very clever. I never said all. I only said sums. Every word was true, so I slept well.
Then one day the teacher sent a note home: "Vasudha's homework is always half finished." My father read it at dinner and didn't shout. He just said quietly, "You never lied to me, did you? You only let me believe." That hurt more than any scolding.
After that, I learned to say, "Five done, five left." Much easier to sleep.

qa.q: How many sums had young Vasudha done out of ten?
qa.a: She had done the first five. There were ten.

qa.q: How did young Vasudha feel when her father spoke quietly at dinner?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, because his quiet words showed her that letting him believe something false was not really clever or honest.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things?
qa.a: Vasudha chose to say "Five done, five left," giving the whole picture instead of hiding the half that wasn't done.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's father have felt reading the teacher's note?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and a little sad, realising his daughter had been leaving things out every night.

grounding: An aunt recalls saying true words about homework while leaving out that it was half done, and learning that silence can mislead.

passage:
The power went out at seven, and Mummy was packing in a hurry for her early train to Pune. "Sonali, homework done?" she called, stuffing clothes into a bag by torchlight.
Sonali looked at her notebook. The English was done. The maths sheet was only half done.
"I did my English, and I did the maths sheet," she said. That was true. She had done some of it.
"Good girl," Mummy said, and kissed her head.
Sonali lay in bed feeling squirmy. She hadn't said anything false. But Mummy thought everything was finished. Was that a lie or not?
In the morning, before Mummy left, Sonali tugged her dupatta. "Mummy, I only did half the maths."
Mummy stopped, smiled and said, "Thank you for telling me all of it. Finish it with Indu aunty next door after school."

qa.q: Which part of the homework was only half done?
qa.a: The maths sheet was only half done.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel lying in bed?
qa.a: Sonali felt squirmy and uneasy, unsure whether leaving out the unfinished part counted as a lie.

qa.q: What did Sonali do in the morning that set things right?
qa.a: She told Mummy she had only done half the maths, giving the whole picture before Mummy left.

qa.q: How did Mummy respond to hearing all of it?
qa.a: Mummy smiled, thanked Sonali for telling all of it, and arranged for the maths to be finished with Indu aunty after school.

grounding: Shows a child giving a true but partial answer about homework and learning that misleading by leaving things out still counts.
